headline: Fed on Track to Raise Interest Rates Next Month And Maybe Again in January
author: Enda Curran

paragraphs.text: (Bloomberg) -- The US monetary policy debate has already moved on to January.
Most Read from Bloomberg

In a blitz of speeches and interviews this week, Federal Reserve officials locked in market expectations for an interest-rate hike in December and opened the prospect of the first back-to-back increases since 2023.
The case for higher rates was given new urgency Tuesday when the October consumer-price report showed inflation accelerated and broadened across everyday goods and services.

"Inflation is far too high," said New York Fed President John Williams, while Chicago Fed's Austan Goolsbee described the data as "borderline disturbing." Dallas Fed President Lorie Logan said officials may need to hike "more rapidly" than she expected, while Fed Governor Christopher Waller went as far as warning that a 50-basis-points move may be needed next month.

"December is clearly locked and loaded for a 25-basis-point hike," said Olu Sonola, head of US economics at Fitch Ratings. "The real questions are how quickly the next hike follows and how many more will ultimately be needed."

About half of the 19 officials who sit on the Federal Open Market Committee, and about half who will vote at the December and January meetings, have spoken over the course of the week. On the last two questions, the signals were mixed.

They ranged from Waller's reference to an outsized move to the Cleveland Fed's Beth Hammack reiterating her preference for more frequent, smaller rises, and Philadelphia Fed President Anna Paulson favoring a gradual pace for increases.

There was more bad news on Friday when data showed wholesale prices, which feed into the Fed's preferred measure of inflation, climbed in October from a year earlier at their fastest pace since 2022. Transportation and warehousing costs jumped, adding to evidence of persistent price pressures throughout the economy.

"It now sounds like there's a worry to get ahead of the re-acceleration and increase the frequency and potentially increase what the FOMC views as terminal," meaning how high the rates should ultimately go, said Michael Reid, head of US economics at the Royal Bank of Canada.

Economists at Bank of America and at Santander US Capital Markets increased the number of hikes they expect following the week of data and the flurry of speeches. Bank of America now sees increases at the next three Fed meetings, while Santander is projecting two raises, in December and March.

The case for caution rests on parts of the economy that are vulnerable to higher borrowing costs, such as the housing market. Economic data this week highlighted how depressed that sector is, with sales of previously owned homes falling last month to a 16-year low.

Boston Fed President Susan Collins on Friday acknowledged that higher interest rates can hurt housing affordability, but added that price stability, in the long run, is more important for housing and the overall economy.

"It does seem to me that the appropriate direction for monetary policy is clear," she said, referring to the need to raise rates. But, in an interview with Bloomberg Television, she stopped short of revealing what she thought would be the right pace.
"I don't want to get ahead in terms of how high we should go or how fast," she said.

Stock market volatility linked to concerns about a slowdown in the artificial intelligence boom is another concern. Fed Governor Michelle Bowman cautioned of risks that include a sharp downturn in share prices if returns on investments in AI fall short of expectations.

"Lower equity prices could undermine the resilience in consumer spending," she said. "And higher interest rates could further strain interest-rate-sensitive sectors of the economy, like housing and small business investment."
Another variable is the potential for a decline in energy prices over coming months that would take pressure off fuel costs and offer relief to households and businesses.
Richmond Fed President Tom Barkin, who spoke on Monday, said rates need to go higher but at a careful pace.

"Most Fed officials seem aligned on the need for hikes and the preference to not rush things," Eric Wallerstein, chief macro strategist for Clocktower Group and previously an adviser to former Fed Governor Stephen Miran.
Fed officials raised rates by a quarter-point in September to a target range of 3.75% to 4%, and then held steady when the FOMC last met in October.

Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh, who hasn't spoken publicly since his October press conference, is due to talk about his task force on AI and productivity at an event on Monday. Few expect him to deviate from his stated preference not to give any guidance on the near-term outlook for policy.
Yet investors aren't waiting and have already priced quarter-point increases in for December, January and March. Before this week, investors had anticipated increases in December and March.

In an example of how jolted markets were by this week's Fed communication, Treasury yields spiked after the remarks from Waller and Logan, who spoke before and after the hotter-than-expected inflation data on Tuesday. The yield on the two-year note rose 19 basis points to 4.75% that day, its largest gain since President Donald Trump's tariff announcements roiled global markets in April 2025.

"The guidance from the Fed is a bit confusing and has sparked large swings in Treasury yields, and again — with Chair Warsh refraining from commenting — others are filling the void," said Nationwide Chief Economist Kathy Bostjancic.

Ultimately, accelerating economic growth may offer cover for the Fed to hike. Data last week showed jobs growth surged in October and the unemployment rate edged lower. Officials will receive one more jobs report and another read of October inflation before they gather again in December.
Few observers expect that set of data will reveal a meaningful slowdown.

"Gradualism is a policy mistake in an economy with strong growth and high inflation," said Robert Sockin, chief US economist at PGIM. "History suggests a high risk that this approach ultimately leads a central bank to need to tighten faster and more overall than it would have had to do otherwise."
